questions.q: What is Salesses's central claim about craft?
choices: Craft is a set of culturally specific expectations
Craft is a set of universal rules
Craft can only be learned by reading the classics
questions.explain: Conventions are built up in particular communities of readers, not laws of nature.

questions.q: Who is the 'default reader' Salesses criticizes?
choices: A supposedly neutral reader who in practice reflects the dominant tradition of American literary fiction
questions.explain: Workshops often judge by this reader's expectations without naming them.

questions.q: A workshop note says, 'Your protagonist is too passive; things just happen to her.' How might Salesses respond?
choices: Ask whose expectations the note reflects; stories shaped by fate or community aren't failures of craft
questions.explain: He sees the demand for individual agency as a cultural value. Compare Baxter, who defends agency.

questions.q: Which is one of his workshop reforms?
choices: The writer can say who the story is for and lead the discussion
Stories are read anonymously and never discussed
questions.explain: He wants feedback to start from the writer's goals.

questions.q: What does Salesses suggest a reader should ask when they think something 'doesn't work'?
choices: For whom, and according to what convention
Whether the sentences are short enough
questions.explain: Making expectations explicit is central to his approach.

questions.q: Which is a fair criticism of Craft in the Real World?
choices: Its picture of 'Western craft' can be a generalization, and some found its reforms modest
questions.explain: Reviewers raised both points, while many still praised the book.

questions.q: Why do some teachers defend the traditional silent workshop?
choices: It mimics a real reader meeting the text without the author present to explain
questions.explain: That is the main defense of the 'gag rule'.

ideas: Craft is not a set of universal laws but a set of expectations built up by particular communities of readers.
Every story has an audience, and a workshop that pretends to a neutral reader is really judging by a dominant one.
The writer whose work is being discussed should speak, say who the story is for, and steer the conversation.
